forces.title: Electrification and data center growth driving increased power transmission demand
forces.description: A structural rise in electricity demand, fueled by increasing electrification across industries (e.g., EVs, heat pumps) and significant data center expansion, is leading to a global surge in grid investment. This directly translates into higher demand for transmission infrastructure, including transformers and HVDC systems, as more electricity flows over longer distances and in new directions. This is a fundamental shift in the operating environment for power transmission.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Renewables integration requires more complex and extensive transmission networks
forces.description: The shift towards renewable energy sources (solar, wind) significantly increases the demand for transmission infrastructure. Renewables are often built far from load centers, requiring longer transmission lines and HVDC systems. Their lower utilization rates and dispersed nature multiply the number of grid connection points and bidirectional power flow requirements, demanding more transformers and a highly interconnected grid. This adds complexity and investment needs to the transmission sector.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Aging grid infrastructure necessitates substantial replacement investment
forces.description: Much of the existing grid infrastructure, particularly in Europe and North America (including the UK), has exceeded its 25- to 40-year design life. Failure rates tend to climb after approximately 30 years of operation, making replacement a significant demand driver for power transmission components like transformers. These replacement units are typically larger due to increased power needs, contributing to sustained grid investment and demand for new equipment.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Severe supply constraints and backlogs in transformer manufacturing
forces.description: The global transformer market is facing significant supply constraints, with a backlog exceeding 1,000 GVA by 2024 and projected to grow to ~1,690 GVA by 2030. Manufacturing is concentrated and slow to expand due to capital intensity, specialized labor, and tight supply of key inputs like grain-oriented electrical steel. This scarcity is most acute in Europe and North America, directly delaying grid build-outs and new capacity additions for power transmission infrastructure.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: Extended lead times and increased prices for critical transmission equipment
forces.description: Due to the sustained scarcity in the transformer market, lead times for these critical components have stretched from historical norms of about one year to up to five years. Concurrently, market prices have surged by over 50% since 2021. This decisively shifts market power from buyers to suppliers, posing a significant risk for utilities and grid operators in Power Transmission, as it delays project timelines, increases capital expenditure, and potentially restricts the acceleration of renewables integration or grid replacements.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

forces.title: HVDC technology enhances efficiency and control in transmission networks
forces.description: High-Voltage DC (HVDC) valves and converter stations are critical for modern transmission networks, increasing efficiency and control for Transmission System Operators (TSOs). HVDC reduces network losses over long distances, supports voltage regulation, reactive power management, and enables interconnecting asynchronous grids. This technology is becoming increasingly important with the accelerating deployment of offshore wind and urban grid connections, offering a key solution for efficient bulk power transfer and grid stability.
forces.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

forces.title: Regulatory action and predictable returns re-incentivize grid infrastructure investment
forces.description: European policymakers are increasingly relying on long-term support mechanisms to encourage investment in capital-intensive energy infrastructure, with governments taking direct stakes in critical energy infrastructure. Regulated grid infrastructure offers more predictable economics compared to the volatile generation market. This shift creates greater revenue and cash flow visibility and more stable, infrastructure-like returns, providing a strong incentive for incumbents and investors to deploy capital into power transmission networks.
forces.source_title: Utilities at an inflection point: Four strategic evolutions ahead

forces.title: UK electricity bills rising due to network costs and declining demand
forces.description: Britain's high electricity bills are increasingly driven by rising fixed network costs (accounting for 86% of the forecast increase by 2035) and a sustained fall in demand since 2015. This creates a negative demand/price spiral where bills suppress demand, which in turn raises unit costs due to the high fixed-cost base of the power system. This structural issue burdens consumers and necessitates significant changes to cost allocation and demand stimulation to improve affordability.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

forces.title: Severe grid congestion delaying connections and increasing constraint costs in UK
forces.description: The UK electricity grid faces severe transmission bottlenecks, with renewable generation concentrated in Scotland and northern England, while demand is focused around London and the South East. This spatial mismatch leads to significant grid congestion, causing projects to wait years for connection. Constraint costs, such as paying Scottish wind farms to curtail output, reached £1.7 billion in 2024/25 and are projected to rise to as much as £8 billion by 2030 if transmission expansion is delayed, highlighting a critical operational and financial challenge.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

forces.title: Grid-positive data centers offer significant potential for UK demand growth
forces.description: Data centers represent the strongest source of near-term, economically additive demand growth for the UK grid, with a potential to add 14GW by 2035. By becoming 'grid-positive' (locating intelligently and operating flexibly), data centers can help cover fixed grid investment costs and reduce consumer bills. This approach involves strategies like non-firm connections with curtailment, a national market for powered land, developer self-build of connections, and using behind-the-meter power as a bridge to full grid capacity, maximizing value to the system.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

forces.title: Policy reforms to alleviate UK consumer bill burdens and stimulate demand
forces.description: BCG proposes a package of policy reforms to improve affordability and stimulate electricity demand in the UK. These include moving social and Renewables Obligation/Feed-in Tariff costs to general taxation, slowing network depreciation to match asset life, utilizing the National Wealth Fund to defer capital-related network charges, and financing new infrastructure more cheaply from the outset using public finance. These measures aim to reallocate costs, reduce immediate bill pressure, and kickstart a positive spiral where costs are recovered across a larger usage base.
forces.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

forces.title: Market power shifting from buyers to suppliers in critical equipment
forces.description: The sustained scarcity in the transformer market, marked by global backlogs and a persistent supply deficit, has fundamentally shifted market power. Manufacturers and suppliers of critical power transmission equipment now command higher prices and extended lead times. This repricing of the market reflects the bottleneck in the value chain, where capacity rather than demand is the binding constraint, signaling a period of elevated costs and procurement challenges for utilities and grid operators.
forces.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

viewpoints.title: Transformer supercycle driven by electrification and aging infrastructure, creating supply-demand imbalance
viewpoints.description: McKinsey identifies a 'transformer supercycle' where global demand is significantly outrunning supply. This is fundamentally reshaping decision-making across the power sector value chain. Increased electrification, data center expansion, and the shift to renewable energy are driving demand for transformers, which are critical for grid connections and build-outs. Supply struggles to keep pace due to manufacturing constraints, leading to a global backlog. This situation has implications for utilities and grid operators, who must secure capacity early to avoid project delays, and for manufacturers who benefit from increased prices and market power.
viewpoints.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply

viewpoints.title: UK electricity bills require higher usage and grid-positive data centers for reduction
viewpoints.description: BCG asserts that to cut Britain's high electricity bills, the country counter-intuitively needs to use more electricity, not less. The current cost structure is burdened by fixed network costs that disproportionately affect consumers due to declining demand. Large new loads, particularly from data centers, are proposed as an economically additive driver that can help cover grid investment, reduce costs for consumers and businesses, and support the UK’s AI ambitions. This requires data centers to be 'grid-positive' by locating intelligently, operating flexibly, and contributing to infrastructure costs.
viewpoints.source_title: To Cut Electricity Bills, Britain Needs to Use More, Not Less

demand_drivers.description: Global mobility, industry, and building systems electrify, increasing demand for efficient and reliable power conversion technologies integral to transmission.

market_sizing.methodology: Global power transmission market value in 2025, with a projection for 2030 and a CAGR. The market includes technologies like HVDC valves and other power conversion equipment essential for transmission networks.
market_sizing.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

demand_drivers.description: Accelerating deployment of HVDC systems to connect offshore wind farms to the grid.
Increased use of HVDC for efficient power delivery and control in urban areas.
Transition to advanced valve technologies (e.g., insulated-gate bipolar transistor) and upgrades of ultra-high-voltage DC systems.

market_sizing.methodology: Global market size for High-Voltage Direct Current (HVDC) valves, which are critical components within HVDC converter stations used in modern transmission networks. The market is forecast to increase to $3.9 billion by 2030.
market_sizing.source_title: The power conversion market: Decarbonization and growth opportunities

demand_drivers.description: Fueled by data centers, electrification of road transport (EVs), buildings, and industry, increasing electricity flow over longer distances and with greater flexibility.
Shift to renewables (solar, wind) requires more transformer capacity per unit of delivered energy due to generation moving away from load centers, lower utilization, and dispersed sites.
Much of the existing grid infrastructure in Europe and North America has exceeded its 25- to 40-year design life, necessitating replacement with often larger units.
Expected to grow at about 3.5% annually, resulting in a 40% increase by 2035, with small and medium power transformers leading growth.

market_sizing.methodology: Analysis of transformer demand drivers, emphasizing that transformers represent an estimated 20 to 25 percent of total transmission capital expenditure. The global grid spending is projected to grow by approximately 4.4 percent annually through 2035, directly translating into rising transformer demand.
market_sizing.source_title: The transformer supercycle: Why demand is outrunning supply
